item.title: Dan Campbell: Lions fans took over the stadium in Arizona
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: Lions head coach Dan Campbell credited the crowd for helping his team in Sunday's win over the Cardinals, even though the Lions were on the road.
item.content:encoded:
Lions head coach Dan Campbell credited the crowd for helping his team in Sunday's win over the Cardinals, even though the Lions were on the road.

Campbell said Lions fans have showed out in each of the last two road games, but they were particularly loud in Arizona, when the Lions won 45-21.

"Our fans were outstanding. They traveled well — they traveled well to Carolina, we just didn't give them anything to cheer about," Campbell said. "They took over that stadium. You could hear them and by the end of it, that was good stuff. We hear them. We hear you. And we love it. We love it."

Lions fans have traveled as well as anyone in the NFL in recent years, routinely making themselves heard in road games. That matters to Campbell.

item.title: Key Korn Ferry document in Brian Flores case becomes public
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Flores adds to his claims against the Dolphins based on statements the team allegedly made about him.
item.content:encoded:
The document that the NFL and search firm Korn Ferry did not want the public to see has now been revealed.

The item is attached to a supplemental complaint filed by Flores against the Miami Dolphins, in his lawsuit that was first filed in February 2022.

The document in question, which is attached as an exhibit to the supplemental complaint, contains a summary of Flores's "strengths and weaknesses," as prepared by Korn Ferry.

The document includes this assessment as one of seven bullet points in the "weaknesses" category: "Needs someone strong at the top to reign [sic] in some of his worst behavior. He once threatened violence to his GM and made irrational demands during an ownership meeting. One long-time senior team executive said, 'He may have changed since, but he was the worst hiring decision we've ever made.' Another President of a club refused to talk about him." (Emphasis added.)

Another bullet point says this: "Ongoing litigation may be a distraction." (Emphasis in original.)

The Raiders, who received that assessment from Korn Ferry, did not interview Flores for the team's head-coaching vacancy on which Korn Ferry was consulting.

The supplemental complaint filed by Flores accuses the Dolphins of making the statement calling him "the worst hiring decision we've ever made."

Flores's lawyers at the firm of Wigdor LLP and Elefterakis, Elefterakis & Panek issued a statement on Tuesday, a copy of which PFT has received.

"The recently unsealed documents demonstrate two unfortunate, but unsurprising, realities," they said. "First, that Mr. Flores’ decision to hold the league and its teams accountable for systemic race discrimination has been met with unlawful retaliation. Second, discrimination continues to play a significant role in the hiring process for NFL Head Coaches, as evidenced by the fact that the candidate profile prepared for the Raiders leans heavily on racial stereotypes. We and Mr. Flores are committed to eradicating the institutional racism and retaliation that permeates the league, its teams and their partners.”

In our view, characterizing Flores as "the worst hiring decision we've ever made" makes it much more difficult for Flores to get a head-coaching job, and it opens the door to the question of whether that assessment was motivated in whole or in part by Flores exercising his prerogative to challenge the decision to fire him via the filing of a lawsuit.

Given the casual manner in which these statements appeared in a formal summary of Flores prepared by Korn Ferry, it's fair to wonder how many other breadcrumbs his lawyers will uncover in the discovery process — especially once they get their hands (and eyes) on informal communications among owners and executives, such as emails and text messages.

item.title: Andy Reid has "not really" been surprised by Kenneth Walker's performances
item.dc:creator: Myles Simmons
item.description: After a Week 5 bye, the Chiefs will be back in action when they play the Chargers on Sunday.
item.content:encoded:
After a Week 5 bye, the Chiefs will be back in action when they play the Chargers on Sunday.

Kenneth Walker likely needed the idle week, as he's racked up 99 touches over his first four games. He’s leading the league at 6.2 yards per carry and 134.3 rushing yards per game.

Has this kind of production surprised Kansas City head coach Andy Reid?

“Yeah, I would tell you not really because we thought he did well, especially when [the Seahawks] had to turn everything over to him during the playoffs,” Reid told reporters in his Monday press conference. "So, we saw his whole game there, and now we're just seeing it on an extended basis where he comes in and he's been able to showcase all that.”

Walker has rushed for at least 170 twice in his first four games with the Chiefs and accumulated at least 175 yards from scrimmage in three of four games. He’s also scored at least two touchdowns in three of four to help Kansas City start the season 4-0.

item.title: Rams' Alaric Jackson punched Bills' Bradley Chubb after game
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: Jackson will be facing NFL discipline for approaching Chubb after the game and throwing a punch.
item.content:encoded:
After his team lost the game, Rams offensive lineman Alaric Jackson lost his cool and punched Bills linebacker Bradley Chubb.

Well after the game was over, while Chubb talked to players on both teams near midfield, Jackson walked over to him and they briefly exchanged words before Jackson threw a right hook to Chubb's jaw. Chubb was unfazed afterward.

"It's just emotions, you know what I mean? Emotional game, it was a close game," Chubb told the California Post. "They always catch the second guy, so I let him swing, and then my teammates held me back, and I just chilled."

Chubb was also seen talking to Rams defensive end Myles Garrett on the field, but when asked whether the two of them had exchanged words, Chubb said there were no issues.

"Just the whole team. Like I said, it was an emotional game. Tempers flared," Chubb said. "But it is what it is. We flushed it and we onto next week."

Chubb didn't mention Jackson by name in his postgame interview.

"Somebody swung, but hey, that's not on me to tell who," Chubb said. "There's cameras out there. I just know, you know what I'm saying, I'm just ready for next week."

Asked if he was OK, Chubb said he's fine.

"I'm just ready for next week," he said. "You see me, I'm smiling, I'm with my team. I'll be ready for next week."

Whether Jackson is playing or suspended next week remains to be seen.

item.content:encoded:
The Eagles won't issue their injury designations for Week 6 until Friday, but defensive coordinator Vic Fangio all but ruled one member of the defense out on Tuesday.

Linebacker Jalyx Hunt left last Sunday's loss to the Jaguars with knee and ankle injuries. Fangio said at his weekly press conference, via multiple reporters, that it would be "miraculous" if Hunt is able to play against the Panthers in Week 6.

Hunt had three tackles and a pass defensed against Jacksonville. He has 15 tackles, a tackle for loss and four quarterback hits on the season.

The Eagles played without Jonathan Greenard in Week 5 due to an ankle injury, so they were down to Nolan Smith, Arnold Ebiketie, and A.J. Epenesa on the edge after Hunt's injury.

item.title: Brian Branch precedent points to a suspension for Alaric Jackson
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: The Rams may not have left tackle Alaric Jackson for Sunday's game against the Cardinals.
item.content:encoded:
The Rams may not have left tackle Alaric Jackson for Sunday's game against the Cardinals. And not because of an injury.

Jackson's decision to punch Bills defensive end Bradley Chubb in the face well after the game ended invites a suspension.

Last year, the NFL imposed a one-game suspension on Lions safety Brian Branch for striking Chiefs receiver JuJu Smith-Schuster with an open hand to the facemask in the immediate aftermath of a Sunday night game.

“Your aggressive, non-football act was entirely unwarranted, posed a serious risk of injury, and clearly violated the standards of conduct and sportsmanship expected of NFL players,” NFL V.P. of football operations Jon Runyan wrote in a letter to Branch, exactly one year ago to the day. “Your conduct reflected poorly on the NFL and has no place in our game.”

On Monday night, Jackson sucker punched Chubb well after the game ended; Chubb's helmet was off, and Jackson had returned to the field after removing his shoulder pads and jersey.

If it had happened outside the stadium, Jackson would have been arrested and charged with assault. (He still could be, technically.) The fact that it happened well after the Monday night game ended could prompt scrutiny under the Personal Conduct Policy, which prohibits (among other things) "[v]iolent or threatening behavior toward another employee or a third party in any workplace setting."

If the NFL proceeds under the Personal Conduct Policy, Jackson's prior violation could prompt something more than a one-game suspension.

Either way, discipline is surely coming for Jackson. Given the precedent set by the Brian Branch case, the punishment should be a suspension of at least one game.

UPDATE 11: 47 a.m. ET: Per the NFL, it's not a Personal Conduct Policy issue. Jackson will be subject to discipline under the normal pregame/in-game/postgame rules.

item.title: Dre Greenlaw suspended for one game
item.dc:creator: Myles Simmons
item.description: The NFL announced on Monday that Greenlaw has been suspended after he headbutted Ernest Jones during Sunday's game.
item.content:encoded:
49ers linebacker Dre Greenlaw has been suspended for one game after his actions during the first half of Sunday’s game against the Seahawks, the NFL announced on Monday.

While he can appeal the suspension, he currently will be eligible to return to San Francisco’s active roster on Tuesday, Oct. 20, as the 49ers play the Commanders on Monday night in Week 6.

While on Seattle’s sideline after a play, Greenlaw used his helmet to headbutt linebacker Ernest Jones, who was not wearing a helmet. The NFL’s announcement notes this was a violation of Rule 12, Section 3, Article 1, which applies to “any act which is contrary to the generally understood principles of sportsmanship.”

Greenlaw was ejected from the game.

Greenlaw was previously suspended one game in 2025 for unsportsmanlike conduct.

If Greenlaw appeals, his suspension would be heard and decided upon by the NFL and NFLPA’s jointly appointed hearing officers: Derrick Brooks, Jordy Nelson, Ron Rivera, or James Thrash.

item.title: Dan Quinn, the day after the clock debacle: "We've got a lot of shit to clean up on"
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: Commanders coach Dan Quinn, who remains employed on Monday, met with reporters for his press conference one day after the most recent game.
item.content:encoded:
Commanders coach Dan Quinn, who remains employed on Monday, met with reporters for his press conference one day after the most recent game. And the most recent game, a 27-27 tie with the Giants, ended with the worst example of clock management in recent years, if not ever.

Quinn began with an opening statement that addressed the woolly mammoth in the mudroom.

"Well, I spoke with the team and with the coaches today, and honestly just like furious about our execution in the crucial moments of the game," Quinn told reporters. "We work really hard on these, and it didn't look like that yesterday. And [I'm] pissed about it.

"So I'll take you through overtime. We wanted to use some clock after getting into field goal range. There has been four kicks that had been missed in the game. So burning some time is the smart call, as you kick near the end of the game.

"About 56 seconds, we handed off to Rachaad White, and it took entirely too long from there on to execute our strategy, from subbing to clock awareness to clocking [the] ball. And when I told the team, and with the coach— like, it was a breakdown. It can't happen. And our time today as a team was spent on the how and the why and make sure that it never does again. So, yesterday's ending was the biggest example, but we've got a lot of shit to clean up on from yesterday's game, and trust me, everyone in this building started with me feels that urgency."

During the question-and-answer phase of the press conference, Quinn was asked whether he has spoken to ownership and whether he's concerned about his job.

"I do know how the league goes," Quinn said. "I'm well aware of that. [Owner] Josh [Harris] and I, we talk regularly before games, after games, after good games, after tough games, and that's a normal process for us. And, trust me, no one is pleased with this outcome and where we're at. The part that we do have, those hard conversations, we're honest about where we're at and what we need to fix and what we need to work on. And so I like having that communication with him."

Implicit in that response is that Quinn has spoken to Harris, that Harris wasn't pleased (as he shouldn't have been), and that Harris did not and won't be firing him, at least for now.

As to the surreal tick-ticking of the clock at the play that began with 55 seconds on the clock and that resulted in the next play beginning with 12 seconds left, Quinn was specifically concerned about the time required to make substitutions and get the play that was called by offensive coordinator David Blough started.

"If you execute it quickly," Quinn said, "then you can get back on the ball and clock it. So the execution of subbing and the slowness of that to go is entirely too long. Hindsight, don't sub, we can get back on the ball with the same group, and do the same outcome. But it wasn't anything unorthodox or unusual, our execution as an entire group in that [55] seconds down to when we weren't able to get it clocked. That's not the play selection, but yet the execution of all of it."

He's correct, but he continues to speak about the situation as if he wasn't standing on the sideline. He was there. He was in position to override whatever was happening. To hit the kill switch on the artificial, I mean, super intelligence. By all appearances, Quinn did nothing other than act as a passive observer.

He later was asked whether the moment will define the season for the Commander.

"I don't catastrophize things, but I do want to make sure that I don't minimize things, either," Quinn said. "And there are plenty of things for us to improve upon in this game, and not just, you know, the last play. And so, I want to make sure I'm always emphasizing that to the team, about what we're capable of, what we need to work on, but by no small margin . . . it was the execution, man. And that's what I want us as players and coaches to absolutely drill down, nail it, because you have this bad taste in your mouth . . . and you want it, like, in our team meeting today, we laid out the plan of how to go play our best at San Francisco. So I do want to make sure I'm expressing what we're teaching, but at the same time, you know, also point to what we need to get done."

What would Quinn say to the fans that have lost confidence in him as the head coach?

"I'm just as pissed, too," Quinn said. "Like, this is a really hard loss, man. And I have a lot of faith in who we are as an organization, ownership, coaching, players, so I'm very much looking forward to get back on the field Monday night."

Of course he is. The only way to put Sunday's debacle behind him will be to beat the 49ers. Who are led by Kyle Shanahan. Who was Quinn's offensive coordinator during the 28-3 debacle in Super Bowl LI, which happened in large part due to another example of Quinn not being able to properly manage the game clock in real time.

Another loss, especially a blowout, could end up being Quinn's final act as head coach of the Commanders — especially with the Commanders' bye coming in Week 7.

item.title: Panthers designate RB Trevor Etienne for return, put DT Cam Jackson on IR
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: Running back Trevor Etienne is on his way back to the Panthers lineup.
item.content:encoded:
Running back Trevor Etienne is on his way back to the Panthers lineup.

The team announced that Etienne has been designated to return from injured reserve. Etienne hurt his ankle in August and became eligible to return to action after Carolina beat the Lions in Week 4, but his 2026 debut had to wait for the team to return from their bye week.

Etienne was a 2025 fourth-round pick and he served as a returner in addition to seeing limited action on offense during his rookie season. Chuba Hubbard and AJ Dillon are the current running backs on the team's 53-man roster.

The Panthers also announced that they have placed defensive tackle Cam Jackson on injured reserve. Jackson has a shoulder injury.

The Jackson move leaves the Panthers with three open slots on their active roster. They've also designated offensive tackle Taylor Moton and defensive lineman Turk Wharton for return this week, so all three could be back for their Week 6 game against the Eagles.

item.title: Did Jayden Daniels think overtime would continue after the first period ended?
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: The problem with everyone taking the blame for a colossal clock-management blunder is that, if everyone is Spartacus, it's impossible to know who's truly at fault.
item.content:encoded:
The problem with everyone taking the blame for a colossal clock-management blunder is that, if everyone is Spartacus, it's impossible to know who's truly at fault.

As to the end of the Giants-Commanders game, coach Dan Quinn has taken the blame — and quarterback Jayden Daniels has taken the blame. Presumably, offensive coordinator David Blough will take the blame, too, the next time he speaks to reporters.

So who's truly to blame?

On Tuesday's edition of PFT Live, Chris Simms suggested that Daniels may have been told to throw the ball away on the last snap the Commanders took. If he had, the clock would have stopped and the Commanders would have had time to kick a potential game-winning field goal. If that's the case, it seems logical that there will be reporting from unnamed sources that the internal review came to that conclusion. (And, again, it would have been easier to get to the bottom of it if the Commanders had recorded and preserved all in-game communications.)

Here's another possibility, one that has a historical example. In 2008, after a 13-13 final score between the Eagles and Bengals, Philadelphia quarterback Donovan McNabb admitted that he didn’t know a regular-season game could end in a tie. He wasn't alone; other players on the Eagles' roster didn't realize the game ended when the overtime period expired.

Said McNabb at the time, who was in his tenth NFL season: "In college, there are multiple overtimes, and in high school and Pop Warner. I never knew in the professional ranks it would end that way. I hate to see what would happen in the Super Bowl and in the playoffs."

Eighteen years later, could it have been déjà vu all over again? Is it possible Daniels's lack of urgency in the final seconds of overtime resulted from the fact that he didn't know the game would be over when the clock struck zero?

Given the Eagles' widespread lack of awareness as to the overtime rules in 2008 — which had been in place unchanged for 34 years — is it crazy to think Daniels and possibly other players didn't know? Likewise, is it beyond the realm of possibility that Blough, who is the same age now as McNabb was then, didn't know? (Blough absolutely should be asked that question, just in case.)

Giants safety Jevon Holland said this after the game: "I mean, even when the clock ran to zero, there was a second where I was like, 'Is it going to go to the second overtime?' I don't know if it was two overtimes or not. I've never been in an overtime tie like this."

That makes it a fair question to ask, of Daniels and other members of the offense. Did he, and others, think that once the time ran out, the teams would change ends and the game would continue?

While hardly an acceptable explanation, it would make the complete lack of urgency as the seconds ticked away a little more understandable.

item.title: Jerry Jones on Dak Prescott's postgame interaction with driver: Fans can express themselves
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott wasn't happy about hearing from a driver after last Thursday's loss to the Buccaneers, but the interaction didn't bother Cowboys owner Jerry Jones.
item.content:encoded:
Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott wasn't happy about hearing from a driver after last Thursday's loss to the Buccaneers, but the interaction didn't bother Cowboys owner Jerry Jones.

The driver said "embarrassing" as Prescott walked by him in an AT&T Stadium tunnel and Prescott replied by sarcastically calling the driver, who does not work for the team, a "tough guy" before adding "get his ass out of here." During an appearance on 105.3 The Fan, Jones said he's fine with people speaking their mind.

“I didn’t pay a lot of attention to it. It doesn’t impact me at all," Jones said. "The driver in question was not an employee. Fans can express themselves and and should express themselves. Whether he was our employee or not, he was a fan it sounds like. So, I'm for our fans expressing themselves."

The rest of Jones's radio appearance focused on what the Cowboys can do on the field to make future expressions from the fanbase a little more positive.

item.title: Report: TreVeyon Henderson has a high-ankle sprain
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: The Patriots are reportedly going to be without running back TreVeyon Henderson for the near future.
item.content:encoded:
The Patriots are reportedly going to be without running back TreVeyon Henderson for the near future.

Henderson left New England's win over the Raiders with an ankle injury and Adam Schefter of ESPN reports that it has been diagnosed as a high-ankle sprain. Henderson does not need surgery to address the injury, but he is expected to miss multiple weeks while he recovers.

Henderson had four carries for 22 yards and one catch for 16 yards before his injury on Sunday. He has 42 carries for 163 yards and a touchdown in four appearances this season.

The Patriots are also expected to be without left tackle Will Campbell due to a knee injury, so there will be some shuffling to do in a couple of areas heading into this Sunday's game against the Jets.

item.title: DeMeco Ryans: Common theme I've heard about Marvin Harrison Jr. is how hard he works
item.dc:creator: Myles Simmons
item.description: The trade to send Marvin Harrison Jr. from the Cardinals to the Texans became official on Monday as the receiver passed his physical.
item.content:encoded:
The trade to send Marvin Harrison Jr. from the Cardinals to the Texans became official on Monday as the receiver passed his physical.

Head coach DeMeco Ryans told reporters in his Monday press conference that the team is excited to add the young wideout.

“He's another really great playmaker,” Ryans said, via transcript from the team. "He's crushed a lot of college records. Got multiple thousand-yard receiving seasons in college. All-American, always been a top receiver when he's been on the field. He has good rapport with C.J. [Stroud] from their time at Ohio State. We're excited to get him in, add another great player to our group.”

Ryans noted that he’s not worried about Harrison picking up a new scheme quickly to impact the club.

“The thing that I've heard from a lot of people speaking about Marvin is he's one of the hardest workers,” Ryans said. “That's the common theme that I've heard from multiple people, how hard of a worker he is. I'm not concerned about him picking up the offense and what he can be able to run for us, the things that he'll be able to do for us offensively. I'm not concerned about it because the kid is a hard worker. He has a great attitude. He's fired up to be here. When you approach it that way, as he will, he'll fit right in.”

Plus, Harrison’s built-in chemistry with Stroud should speed up that process. Ryans noted the team solicited Stroud’s input on Harrison before executing the deal.

“I hope so,” Ryans said. “I think anytime you have players who have spent time together, whether it's college or other teams, just having that prior relationship definitely helps when you come into a new situation.”

The No. 4 overall pick of the 2024 draft, Harrison’s production to this point of his career has not matched that draft status. After catching 62 passes for 885 yards with eight touchdowns as a rookie, he had 41 receptions for 608 yards with four touchdowns in 12 games last season.

He caught just five passes for 85 yards with a TD in four games this year before the trade.

item.title: Cowboys DC Christian Parker will coach from the booth rather than the sideline
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: The Cowboys brought Mike Pettine in as a senior defensive assistant on Monday and that's not the only change they'll be making as they try to improve their defensive performance over the final 12 games.
item.content:encoded:
The Cowboys brought Mike Pettine in as a senior defensive assistant on Monday and that's not the only change they'll be making as they try to improve their defensive performance over the final 12 games.

During an appearance on 105.3 The Fan on Tuesday, Cowboys owner Jerry Jones said that the team has been searching "for what we can do differently that would give us better results." One of the things they've settled on is moving defensive coordinator Christian Parker from the sideline to the booth on gamedays.

"We’re gonna coach the defense not on the field, but up above. Parker’s going up above," Jones said.

Jones said that the changes are not a sign that they believe Parker is overwhelmed in his first year as the coordinator, but the defense has looked overwhelmed far too often and Jones will eventually run out of levers to pull in hopes of finding a way to fix a unit that the team expected to be much better than it has been thus far.

item.title: PFT's Week 6 2026 NFL power rankings
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: The Niners hold the top spot.
item.content:encoded:
1. 49ers (last week No. 1; 5-0): Plenty of other teams wish they'd made a run at signing Mike Evans.

2. Chiefs (No. 2; 4-0): They've got a chance to deliver the death blow to the Chargers' season.

3. Jaguars (No. 3; 4-1): On a Sunday that featured plenty of lessons, Jacksonville's contribution was to highlight the importance of having a backup long snapper.

4. Bills (No. 4; 3-1): Joe Brady wasn't going to eff around and find out by trying to get the game-winning field goal closer.

5. Seahawks (No. 5; 3-2): They're trying too hard to be something other than they were in 2025.

6. Vikings (No. 8; 5-0): As the offense improves, the Vikings go from "contender" to "threat."

7. Broncos (No. 6; 3-2): When Seattle comes to town on Thursday night, everyone will find out whether this team is a true candidate to get to the Super Bowl.

8. Ravens (No. 10; 4-1): The Ravens still look like the Ravens, even after a coaching change.

9. Patriots (No. 13; 3-2): The patriotic pigeons had a field day on Tom Brady's statue.

10. Rams (No. 7; 2-3): They have five winnable games before the bye; if they lose any of them, things could get interesting down the stretch.

11. Packers (No. 23; 3-2): When your adversary keeps talking, stay quiet and wait for your opportunity.

12 (tie). Browns (No. 12; 3-2): They're first in the list because they beat the Steelers.

12 (tie). Steelers (No. 14; 3-2): They're second in the list because they beat the Bengals.

12 (tie). Bengals (No. 15; 3-2): The win over the Dolphins shouldn't have come down to an onside kick.

15. Bears (No. 9; 3-2): Tyson Bagent's expiration date seems to have arrived.

16. Raiders (No. 11; 3-2): At what point will Fernando Mendoza become the better option to lead a run to a possible playoff berth?

17. Giants (No. 16; 3-1-1): Dan Quinn saved John Harbaugh and Cam Skattebo from being the pin cushions of talk radio in New York.

18. Panthers (No. 19; 2-2): They could win the division by default, again.

19. Eagles (No. 17; 2-3): A bad week ended in the worst way possible.

20. Cowboys (No. 18; 2-3): The arrival of Mike Pettine is both an acknowledgement that the defense needs help and a failure to acquire the kind of help it needs.

21. Lions (No. 21; 2-3): Nothing helps a bad defense like playing a bad offense.

22. Falcons (No. 20; 2-3): Michael Penix Jr. has a long way to go to show that he's sufficiently durable to be a franchise quarterback.

23. Colts (No. 22; 2-3): It feels like an overhaul is inevitable.

24. Texans (No. 24; 1-4): They still have a long way to go to become the team that they were in 2025.

25. Saints (No. 25; 1-4): Three straight home losses may be very hard to overcome.

26. Jets (No. 28; 2-3): Geno Smith has gone from leading the league in interceptions to throwing none.

27. Buccaneers (No. 30; 1-4): They may have found something in Jalon Daniels.

28. Commanders (No. 26; 1-3-1): The clock is still ticking on Dan Quinn. In more ways than one.

29. Cardinals (No. 27; 1-4): The Week 1 win over the Chargers becomes less impressive by the week.

30. Chargers (No. 29; 0-5): The price for a potential Justin Herbert trade is dropping by the week.

31. Titans (No. 31; 0-5): The constant turnover in the organization feels like Game of Thrones meets the Island of Misfit Toys.

32. Dolphins (No. 32; 0-5): Maybe Jon-Eric Sullivan and Jeff Hafley should have waited a year.

item.title: Ladd McConkey was active for "emergency situation" in Week 5, could return in Week 6
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: Chargers wide receiver Ladd McConkey was not on the team's inactive list for Sunday's loss to the Broncos, but he never got on the field.
item.content:encoded:
Chargers wide receiver Ladd McConkey was not on the team's inactive list for Sunday's loss to the Broncos, but he never got on the field.

McConkey missed practice all last week with a foot injury and was listed as questionable on the team's final injury report. That report was a long one and it included six players who were ruled out ahead of Sunday. The Chargers also deactivated cornerback Rodney Shelley, who joined McConkey in the questionable category and head coach Jim Harbaugh said on Monday that the team did not want the wideout on the field unless extreme circumstances demanded it.

"He was an emergency situation. We did not want to put him in," Harbaugh said, via the team's website.

McConkey played a limited role in Week 4 and went without a catch in the team's loss to the Seahawks. He has 12 catches for 183 yards and a touchdown this season.

Harbaugh said it is possible that McConkey will be "working back in" for this week's game against the Chiefs.

item.title: Cam Ward: I'm not a loser, you've got to go through stuff to get wins
item.dc:creator: Myles Simmons
item.description: Cam Ward has been in the league for one full season and five games.
item.content:encoded:
Cam Ward has been in the league for one full season and five games.

To this point, there’s been a lot of losing.

Ward — who has started every game since being selected as No. 1 overall last year — now carries a 3-19 record after Sunday’s 26-3 loss to the Texans. While Tennessee started the game with a field goal, the team failed to score on its last eight possessions.

The results prompted a question at the end of Ward’s postgame press conference: Have you gotten used to losing?

“No, I’m not a loser,” Ward said. “The record may say that we are that right now. But at the end of the day, you’ve got to go through some stuff to try to get wins. And, I mean, we attack this each and every day. But I mean, for that, no.

“If you’re able to look at everybody in our locker room’s track record, we’ve all won games at a high level. And we’re looking forward to doing that in the long run.”

And Ward isn’t shying away from the responsibility that comes with being a No. 1 overall pick and a starting quarterback.

“I just try to continue to do my job,” Ward said. “At the end of the day, I have a lot of stuff to continue to get better at. I think that’s going to put us in positions to win games, the more I can do my job the right way. But everybody in the building knows, it’s going to take all 11 of us on offense to get things how we want it. But I know as far as my job, there’s still a lot of stuff that I need to clean up. I have to continue to motivate my guys the way they need to be motivated. I have to continue to lead my style. And I think if we keep doing that, if we keep on making progress forward, like I know we can, the wins will eventually come.

“I love the criticism. I love everything that comes with the quarterback territory,” Ward added. “At the end of the day, it’s the best position in the world. Stuff goes the right way, you take all the credit. Stuff goes the wrong way, you take all the blame. I know I’m capable at this position. I have the right guys around me to uplift me and myself uplift them. And we’re going to eventually put it together.”

item.title: Cowboys hire Mike Pettine as a defensive assistant
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: The Cowboys' search for ways to help their defense improve has led them to Mike Pettine.
item.content:encoded:
The Cowboys' search for ways to help their defense improve has led them to Mike Pettine.

Head coach Brian Schottenheimer said at a Monday press conference that the team has hired Pettine to serve as a senior defensive assistant. Pettine has worked with both Schottenheimer and defensive coordinator Christian Parker in the past.

Pettine was the defensive coordinator for the Jets from 2009-2012 and Schottenheimer ran the team's offense for the first three of those seasons. Pettine moved on to run the Bills defense the next year and was the Browns' head coach in 2014 and 2015. He served as the Packers' defensive coordinator from 2018-2020 and Parker was a quality control coach in Green Bay for the final two years of that run.

Pettine was most recently the assistant head coach and outside linebackers coach in Minnesota. He parted ways with the Vikings after the 2025 season.

The Cowboys are 2-3 after last Thursday's loss to the Buccaneers. They rank 26th in points allowed and 31st in yards allowed this season.

item.title: Teams should record and save all headset communications
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: When a plane crashes, the "black box" preserves all evidence regarding the cockpit conversations.
item.content:encoded:
When a plane crashes, the "black box" preserves all evidence regarding the cockpit conversations. When an NFL team has an inexplicable failure of coaching, is there a way to go back and listen to how it all happened?

While some teams may preserve that data, the Commanders do not.

Coach Dan Quinn was asked that specific question on Monday, one day after a disastrous failure to manage the final seconds of overtime against the Giants.

"We don't do specifically that," Quinn said. "We do a writeup and then go back and review conversations, situations, the film, and the R&D department goes along with that. As far as the communications go, I want to make sure that's up for me, you know, at the top, this is what's happening. This is what we need to get done. And we'll continue to work really hard on that. We have definitely ways to simulate it. That's one way that we have, and we'll continue to do."

It would make sense to preserve the headset communications, if only for the benefit of ownership to get to the raw and undeniable facts at a time when folks may be looking for ways to cover their butts.

Of course, if owner Josh Harris was on the sideline during games, he'd have first-hand evidence as to what transpired. Which is what Colts owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon does, even though some feel compelled to criticize her for it.

For the owners who aren't on the sideline, preserving those communications should be a no-brainer. If they aren't already doing it, adopting that system could be the equivalent of all teams incorporating victory formation after the disastrous Joe Pisarcik moment from 1978.

item.title: With 210 yards passing and 121 rushing, Josh Allen had his fourth career double-triple
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: Allen reached triple-digit yardage in two statistical categories for the fourth time.
item.content:encoded:
Bills quarterback Josh Allen's spectacular performance in Monday night's win over the Rams was the fourth double-triple of his NFL career.

Allen had 10 carries for 121 yards and a touchdown, and he also completed 12 of 19 passes for 210 yards, with one touchdown and one interception. The Bills won 37-34 in overtime.

A double-triple is PFT’s stat recognizing a player who has triple-digit yardage in two different statistical categories. Allen previously had back-to-back double triples in two 2018 games, with 231 passing and 135 rushing in Week 13 against the Dolphins and 206 passing and 101 rushing in Week 14 against the Jets. He also had 308 passing and 109 rushing in Week 14 of 2021 against the Buccaneers.

The NFL's all-time leader in double-triples is Lamar Jackson, who has accomplished the feat 17 times — more than twice as many as anyone else in NFL history. Michael Vick, with eight double-triples, is second.

The only other double-triple in the NFL this season was accomplished by Jayden Daniels on Sunday, when he had 199 yards passing and 103 yards rushing in the tie against the Giants, when his statistical achievements were overshadowed by his clock management blunder on the last play of the game.

item.title: Rams have consistently under-invested in special teams under Sean McVay and Les Snead
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: Another bad special teams performance doomed the Rams on Monday night.
item.content:encoded:
The most pivotal game of the 2025 regular season turned on a special teams play: With the Rams leading the Seahawks 30-14 in the fourth quarter in Week 16, Seattle's Rashid Shaheed took a punt return and raced 58 yards for a touchdown, sparking a comeback that saw the Seahawks ultimately win 38-37 in overtime.

That game proved to be massive: It was the reason the Seahawks won the NFC West and got to play the Rams at home in the NFC Championship Game on their way to winning the Super Bowl. If the Rams had beaten the Seahawks, the two teams would have finished with the same record and the Rams would have won the tiebreaker, so it would have been the Rams winning the division and only needing to win two home games to reach the Super Bowl. A playoff rematch against the Seahawks would have been in Los Angeles, not Seattle.

Rams coach Sean McVay knew at the time how big that loss was, and afterward he fired his special teams coordinator, Chase Blackburn. Perhaps McVay should have put the blame elsewhere.

McVay, who again pointed the finger at his special teams following another overtime loss on Monday night against the Bills, has worked with General Manager Les Snead on building a team that has consistently under-invested in special teams. McVay keeps replacing special teams coordinators, but the special teams coordinator doesn't pick the players, he just does his best with the players picked for him. And the Rams, who love trading draft picks for big name players on offense and defense, have decided not to invest significant resources into acquiring special teams players.

This offseason, Mike Sando of TheAthletic.com did an analysis of NFL teams and how much they prioritize special teams. The analysis covered five factors: The number of players on each team's roster whose primary role was special teams, whether roster depth spots were used primarily on special teams, the degree to which depth players played special teams over offense or defense, the number of players who were active on game day but played few snaps, and how often starters also regularly played special teams.

In all five categories, the Rams were near the bottom of the league. The Seahawks put significantly more roster resources into special teams players, by all five of those measures.

Shahid is a prime example of how Seattle has an organizational philosophy of investing in special teams. At last year's trade deadline, the Seahawks sent a fourth-round pick and a fifth-round pick to the Saints for Shaheed. It's not hindsight to say the Seahawks changed their season with that trade; we were saying that before Seattle won the Super Bowl. It's also not unreasonable to think that if it had been the Rams, not the Seahawks, who traded for Shaheed, it might have been the Rams who won the Super Bowl last season.

The Rams did try to change things this offseason by signing Grant Stuard primarily for his contributions on special teams. Stuard is listed as a linebacker but has not played any snaps on defense this season, instead playing in all five games exclusively on special teams. So it's fair to say the Rams at least tried to fix their special teams issues this offseason.

But it clearly wasn't enough. The Rams have been the favorites to win the Super Bowl all year. If they fall short, it may be the special teams that deserves the blame — and it may be time for the Rams to ask themselves why the special teams are always taking the blame, year after year.

item.title: Puka Nacua: We have to look in the mirror and say what our identity will be
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: The Rams produced a lot of eye-popping numbers on Monday night, including a career-high 17 catches for wide receiver Puka Nacua, but the most important ones weren't positive ones for the team.
item.content:encoded:
The Rams produced a lot of eye-popping numbers on Monday night, including a career-high 17 catches for wide receiver Puka Nacua, but the most important ones weren't positive ones for the team.

Those would be a 37-34 final score that favored the Bills and the 2-3 record that the Rams are left with thanks to the result. That's not the result you'd expect for a team that gained 454 yards and picked up 33 first downs over the course of the evening, but Nacua's message after the game was that the Rams can't afford to wallow in a painful loss because they'll be back on the field before they know it.

“It’s Monday night. We gotta be able to physically and mentally reset by tomorrow and get ready to play back here at home," Nacua said, via Eric Williams of Fox Sports. "We got the Arizona Cardinals, a familiar face coming in with Mike LaFleur, but it's gonna be an opportunity for us to respond and really look ourselves in the mirror and say, what is our identity gonna be? And can't let the Buffalo Bills beat us twice.”

The final margin can be attributed to a pair of miscues in the kicking game as Harrison Mevis missed one field goal and had his game-winning try in overtime blocked by Bills linebacker Greg Rousseau. Rams head coach Sean McVay pointed in that direction after the game, but the Rams offense and defense could have both finished things without relying on special teams that have regularly disappointed in Los Angeles. Honing that part of their identity would be a good start to making the team's record a little better to look at in the coming weeks.

item.content:encoded:
On Monday night in L.A., Bills quarterback Josh Allen got his 100th career win. He also got his first in overtime.

Allen had been 0-7 in overtime entering the Week 5 game against the Rams. Thanks to a blocked field goal by defensive end Gregory Rousseau and Allen's own legs on the ensuing drive, the Bills moved to 4-1 with a 38-35 victory.

Allen, who had 121 rushing yards, becomes the fourth quarterback to win 100 games in his ninth season. The others were Patrick Mahomes (112), Russell Wilson (107), and Tom Brady (101).

The victory also keeps the Bills in first place. A loss would have dropped Buffalo to 3-2 and, technically, into second place by virtue of losing last week to the Patriots.

On Sunday, the Bills face the 3-2 Raiders in Las Vegas. They're off in Week 7. Next comes a home game against the 4-1 Ravens followed by a Monday night date with the 5-0 Vikings in Minnesota.

item.title: Monday Night Football: Bills beat Rams 37-34 in overtime in instant classic
item.dc:creator: Charean Williams
item.description: Bills kicker Tyler Bass made a 45-yard field goal with 1:55 remaining in OT for the win.
item.content:encoded:
The Bills and Rams were a popular preseason pick to meet in the Super Bowl. If Monday night was a preview, Super Bowl LXI will be a good one.

The heavyweights went back-and-forth on Monday night, with eight lead changes and 35 combined fourth-quarter points.

The game, appropriately, was decided in overtime.

Bills kicker Tyler Bass made a 45-yard field goal with 1:55 remaining in overtime for a 37-34 victory. The Bills are 4-1 and the Rams 2-3.

The first half was all defense as the teams combined for 270 total yards, one play over 20 yards, 20 points, one punt, one turnover and one missed field goal. The second half was all Josh Allen and Matthew Stafford as the quarterbacks took over.

The teams ended up combining for 71 points and 890 yards.

Both teams had chances to win it late in regulation and again in overtime.

James Cook's 5-yard touchdown run with 1:39 remaining in the fourth quarter gave the Bills a brief 34-27 lead, with Buffalo burning 5:35 of the final 7:14. It left plenty of time for Stafford, who led the Rams on an eight-play, 63-yard drive in only 1:34. Rams running back Kyren Williams' 1-yard touchdown run with 5 seconds left tied it 34-34 and sent it to overtime.

The Rams won the toss in overtime and chose to kickoff.

On their first drive, the Bills faced a second-and-16 after a holding penalty. Khalil Shakir then had a 57-yard catch-and-run to the Los Angeles 22 before Rams safety Kamren Kinchens made the touchdown-saving tackle. On the next play, Cook fumbled for the second time. His teammates saved him on the first one but not on the second.

Rams linebacker Nate Landman punched the ball out and defensive lineman Aaron Donald recovered at the 20. Officials missed Landman removing his helmet in the field of play, which should have been a 15-yard penalty.

The Rams then drove 50 yards in eight plays to the Buffalo 30 before kicker Harrison Mevis missed for a second time. Greg Rousseau blocked Mevis' 48-yard attempt.

Allen directed the game-winning drive, with the Bills going 35 yards in five plays. Allen had runs of 19 and 13 on the game-winning drive, and he finished his night with 10 carries for 121 yards and a touchdown.

He was 12-of-19 for 210 yards passing with a touchdown and an interception. Cook ran for 111 yards and two touchdowns on 25 carries.

The Rams outgained the Bills 454 to 436, with Puka Nacua setting a career-high and a Monday Night Football record with 17 catches for 138 yards and a touchdown. Nacua had 24 targets.

Stafford was 40-of-54 for 383 yards and three touchdowns.

Blake Corum and Kyren Williams each had a rushing touchdown, and Davante Adams caught two touchdown passes.

item.title: Sean McVay: Field goal unit "cost us the game tonight"
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: The Rams fell to 2-3 on Monday night, due in part to a couple of missed field goals from kicker Harrison Mevis — including a blocked field goal in overtime that, if good, would have won the game.
item.content:encoded:
The Rams fell to 2-3 on Monday night, due in part to a couple of missed field goals from kicker Harrison Mevis — including a blocked field goal in overtime that, if good, would have won the game.

After the game, Rams coach Sean McVay pointed a finger directly at the field-goal unit after the 38-35 overtime loss: "It cost us the game tonight," McVay told reporters.

McVay then said, "I'm gonna evaluate everything."

Last year, McVay fired special-teams coordinator Chase Blackburn after the Thursday night overtime classic in Seattle. This time around, several folks should be getting a little nervous about whether the pink slip could be coming for them.

The clock is ticking. The next game is on Sunday, against the Cardinals. After that, the Rams visit the Raiders, followed by a home game against the Chargers.

All are winnable, which could boost the Rams to 5-3. Regardless, 2-3 (and 1-3 in prime time) is a far cry from where anyone thought the Rams would be after Week 5.

item.title: Report: Jaguars OT Anton Harrison to have knee surgery
item.dc:creator: Josh Alper
item.description: The Jaguars won't have left tackle Anton Harrison in the lineup against the Texans in Week 6 and it's unclear when he will be back in action.
item.content:encoded:
The Jaguars won't have left tackle Anton Harrison in the lineup against the Texans in Week 6 and it's unclear when he will be back in action.

Harrison injured his knee during the team's win over the Eagles in London in Week 5 and he is set to have arthroscopic surgery to repair his injury. Ian Rapoport of NFL Media reports that his return timeline will be determined once doctors see the extent of the damage to his knee.

Per the report, Harrison could be out for about 3-5 weeks or he could be out for the rest of the season.

Walker Little replaced Harrison on Trevor Lawrence's blind side against the Eagles and will be set to hold down the spot as long as Harrison is unavailable.

item.title: Josh Allen "trusting our guys to be pros" while staying West on a short week
item.dc:creator: Michael David Smith
item.description: The Bills are not traveling home after beating the Rams on Monday night, and that means they need to be totally focused on the job at hand, according to quarterback Josh Allen.
item.content:encoded:
The Bills are not traveling home after beating the Rams on Monday night, and that means they need to be totally focused on the job at hand, according to quarterback Josh Allen.

After playing in Los Angeles on Monday night, the Bills play in Las Vegas on Sunday afternoon, and Allen said on ESPN late Monday night that Buffalo will have an unusual week of practice away from their facility.

"Coming across the country, playing on a Monday night, we're on a short week, we've got to go to Vegas next week," Allen said. "We're staying here. Trusting our guys to be pros and do the right thing. We're here to win this week and next week, and we've got to get past this one on a short week and find a way to win."

After some tough travel logistics ahead of Week 6, the Bills will get to relax with their Week 7 bye before playing at home against the Ravens in Week 8.

item.title: Dolphins coach Jeff Hafley isn't considering benching QB Malik Willis
item.dc:creator: Mike Florio
item.description: The 0-5 Dolphins enter their bye week searching for answers.
item.content:encoded:
The 0-5 Dolphins enter their bye week searching for answers. One of them won't be benching the starting quarterback.

Coach Jeff Hafley was asked by reporters on Monday whether he's thinking about flipping from Malik Willis to Kyle McCord in Week 7.

"No," Hafley said.

He was asked for his thinking in that regard.

"We've played five games and Malik is our quarterback," Hafley said.

"[A]s far as the Malik questions, again, I totally respect all the questions and I get everybody has a job to do, so good question," Hafley said. "We need to be better. Malik needs to be better, OK? And that's not the headline. The headline is we all need to be better, and I mean that. I thought yesterday for the first time we ran the ball really well and we moved the ball. We ran for 200 yards against a really good team. But everything in the pass game has to be better, right? It's the receivers, it's the tight ends, it's the protection. It all has to tie in and it all has to be better. And that's the quarterback, that's the coaches, that's the offensive line, that's the running backs, that's the tight ends. This is a team game that we all need to be more efficient and we need to be better. And we will work through that. I have confidence in the coaches, I have confidence in the players that we have. We will work through that and we will get better. It's been five weeks."

In five games as the Miami starter, Willis has completed 73 of 130 passes for 849 yards, with two touchdowns and four interceptions. His passer rating is 68.4, which puts him last among all 29 qualifiers.
